title: Foreword
text:
📜 You're reading the full verbatim manuscript mirror . View the condensed, interactive edition →
There are moments in history when an industry reaches a turning
point, not because technology failed or the markets dried up, but
because the gap between ambition and execution became too costly to
ignore. I believe the renewable energy industry is living through one of
those moments right now. And I believe this book arrives at exactly the
right time to help us close that gap.
When I founded SunEdison more than two decades ago, we were trying to
solve what seemed like a financing problem. How do you get solar onto
rooftops at scale when the upfront cost is prohibitive? The
solar-as-a-service model unlocked a market that has since grown beyond
anything we dared imagine at the time. But what I learned from that
experience, and from every chapter of my career, is that the hardest
part of the energy transition is never the idea. It is the relentless,
disciplined work of turning that idea into a project that gets built,
financed, and connected to the grid. That work happens in the land
offices, the title reviews, the due diligence rooms, and the negotiating
sessions with county commissions and tribal authorities.
This is Kimberlee Centera’s world. And this book is her gift to
everyone who wants to succeed in it.
Over more than thirty years, Kimberlee has done the work that makes
the energy transition real. Not the announcements. Not the ribbon
cuttings. The work. She has guided Fortune 500 companies and independent
developers through hundreds of transactions, across gigawatts of solar,
wind, storage, and transmission projects, with more than $25 billion in
financed value. She has seen what derails deals and what saves them. She
has sat across the table from landowners who believe they control
property their children already inherited. She has watched projects
collapse at closing because a single signature was missing. She has
navigated the mineral rights dispute nobody saw coming, the municipal
road reservation buried in a decades-old title record, and the tribal
artifacts mistaken for rock piles on a Wyoming site. She has done this
work in good policy environments and difficult ones, and she has emerged
with something rare: a clear-eyed, battle-tested understanding of what
it actually takes to move a project from development to deployment.
What she has written here is not a theoretical framework. It is a
field guide. It is the kind of book that could only be written by
someone who has lived through the consequences of getting this work
wrong, and who has built the expertise to get it right.
I want to place this book in the context of the larger challenge we
face, because I think it deserves that framing.
The clean energy transition is the greatest economic transformation
of our lifetimes. The opportunity is staggering in terms of investment,
jobs, infrastructure, and the long-term competitiveness of the American
economy. We have the technology. We have the expertise. We have, despite
the policy turbulence of recent years, an enduring market logic that
makes renewable energy the rational choice across an ever-expanding set
of applications. For years, clean energy has been 90% of everything
added to the grid, and load growth requires us to be faster.
During my time leading the Loan Programs Office within the U.S.
Department of Energy I watched intelligent, well-funded teams stumble
over the same categories of problems that Kimberlee addresses in these
pages. Land control that hadn’t been properly verified. Ownership
structures that hadn’t been fully mapped. Environmental issues that
emerged too late. Mineral rights that surfaced at closing. Due diligence
that had been compressed to fit a timeline rather than expanded to fit
the risk. In every case, the technology worked. The economics were
sound. The vision was real. What was missing was the operational
discipline to bridge the gap between what a project could become and
what it actually was.
I am particularly moved by Kimberlee’s attention to the human
dimensions of this work, the landowners, the tribal communities, the
local officials, the neighbors who live within sight of a project they
may or may not have been consulted about. The energy transition is not
an abstraction. It unfolds on real land, in real communities, with real
stakeholders whose interests, concerns, and rights must be understood
and respected. Projects that ignore this reality do not just encounter
delays, they forfeit the moral authority that should accompany the work
of building a cleaner world. Kimberlee understands this. Her approach to
community engagement, landowner communication, and stakeholder
collaboration reflects a vision of energy development that is not merely
transactional but genuinely relational.
To the investors and capital allocators who will read this book: I
want to speak to you directly. The clean energy investment landscape has
matured enormously over the past decade, and the sophistication of the
capital flowing into this sector is genuinely impressive. But capital
sophistication does not automatically translate into project discipline.
I have seen too many transactions where the financial engineering was
impeccable, and the term sheet was structured with precision while the
land agreements beneath it were shot through with risk. The message of
this book is that the quality of the underlying asset determines the
quality of every instrument built on top of it. Title insurance, tax
equity, project finance, debt structures all rest on the foundation that
Kimberlee describes. Build a strong foundation. Demand it from the
developers and the teams you back. It is not overhead. It is the
work.
To the developers: you are the heroes of this story, and I mean that
without irony. The people who go out and identify a site, negotiate a
lease, navigate a permitting process, build community support, and bring
a project to financial close are performing one of the most complex and
consequential acts in the modern economy. This book will make you better
at it. Not because it tells you something you could not eventually learn
from experience, but because it compresses decades of hard-won knowledge
into a form you can actually use before you make the expensive mistakes.
Read it before you acquire a project whose previous developer’s work you
do not fully understand.
To the project teams, the title professionals, the environmental
consultants, the legal counsel, the engineers, and every other
specialist who makes up the ecosystem around a renewable energy
transaction: Kimberlee has written a book that honors your work. The
disciplines she describes are not support functions. They are the core
of what makes this industry function. The more clearly the whole
ecosystem understands that, the better the outcomes for everyone.
We are in a race. The world needs us to move faster and to do that we
need to get things right the first time. In that race, execution is
everything. Bankable projects are everything. The knowledge in this book
is important.
Kimberlee Centera has spent thirty years acquiring that knowledge so
that the rest of us can benefit from it. She has written it down with
clarity, precision, and the unmistakable authority of someone who has
earned every lesson the hard way.
The energy transition needs more of this. More rigor. More
discipline. More willingness to do the unglamorous work that separates a
project that closes from a project that doesn’t. More people who
understand that vision without execution is just a press release.
This book is a call to that standard. I am proud to help introduce it
to the world.
Jigar Shah , Co-founder, SunEdison, Former Director,
Loan Programs Office, U.S. Department of Energy, Co-founder,
Multiplier

title: Introduction: Why Mergers and Acquisitions are Shaping the Renewable Energy Future
text:
📜 You're reading the full verbatim manuscript mirror . View the condensed, interactive edition →
The renewable energy sector is evolving rapidly, with mergers and
acquisitions (M&A) activities playing a pivotal role in shaping the
industry’s future. This trend reflects the industry’s maturation and the
increasing complexity of developing large-scale renewable projects.
Since entering the renewable energy industry over 30 years ago, I
have often seen projects change ownership two or three times before
reaching commercial operation. Recently, there has been an upsurge in
M&A activity. The termination and restriction of certain Inflation
Reduction Act (IRA) tax credits and loan guarantees is impacting
renewable energy M&A activity. It has increased deal-making as
companies navigate valuation pressure and look for strategic
consolidations. It reshapes financing, pushing players toward more
risk-hedged, structured deals. And it creates a divide between projects
that locked in credits early and those now struggling under new
rules.
What we are experiencing now has far-reaching implications. Among
them are the following:
1. Policy Changes & Immediate Effects
Policy changes such as the “One Big Beautiful Bill” (OBBB), enacted
on July 4, 2025, alter or eliminate certain tax credits that were
established by the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA). It also adds Foreign
Entity of Concern (FEOC) restrictions to remaining credits. An Executive
Order directs Treasury to tighten the definition of “beginning of
construction.”
2. Heightened Uncertainty
The elimination of commonly used safe harbors has thrown eligibility
standards into flux, creating ambiguity around what qualifies—causing a
rush among developers to accelerate project timelines before credits
vanish. Analysts estimate that up to 29 GW of wind and solar projects
could fail to meet these tightened deadlines, with as much as 122 GW and
$211 billion investment at risk due to the combined effect of
phase-outs, tariffs, and regulatory constraints.
1. Shift toward Opportunistic Acquisitions
With valuations under pressure and financing risk rising for startups
and mature projects alike, acquisition activity has surged. Strategic
buyers are capitalizing on lower project valuations to make
opportunistic purchases. Investors are increasingly favoring “boring but
bankable” assets—projects with proven cash flows, minimal risk of
policy-related disruption—over speculative, subsidy-reliant
technologies.
2. Rise of Sophisticated Capital Structures
Rather than straightforward equity rounds, stakeholders are turning
to layered financing: project finance, debt instruments, preferred
equity, or recapitalizations to avoid diluting ownership and remain
attractive to potential acquirers.
3. Strong Underlying Fundamentals Help Sustain M&A
Despite policy reversals, high electricity demand, especially from
data centers and electrification trends, continues to support the
business case for renewables. Certain tax credits, notably the
Investment Tax Credit (ITC) and Production Tax Credit (PTC) applicable
to projects initiated before 2025, continue to be available, thereby
supporting the preservation of value and reliability for qualifying
initiatives.
Investors are acquiring assets at lower valuations due to policy
uncertainty. Projects with safe-harbored tax credits retain value;
others face steep discounting. Yet rising electricity demand sustains
long-term viability, even with policy risks.
My work with developers, investors, landowners, and other
stakeholders has given me exposure to a wide range of issues that can
arise throughout the project lifecycle. Simple oversights can derail the
entire project or result in costly delays. About 40% of M&A deals
fail, often due to overlooked details discovered only at closing. As
companies strive to meet ambitious pipeline goals and capitalize on
emerging opportunities, understanding M&A best practices becomes
essential.
Land is a fundamental asset for renewable projects. It is imperative
to verify land control to ensure that the project rests on solid ground
– literally and legally. Issues may occur if land control details are
not meticulously managed, promptly addressed, or adequately considered.
Land issues can delay deals, increase legal costs, and disrupt timelines
just before closing. Verifying land control is a critical step that
safeguards the investment and ensures that the project’s foundation is
secure. It is a painstaking process, yet understanding potential
pitfalls can arm your team with the tools to identify and mitigate
risk.
As companies strive to meet ambitious pipeline goals and capitalize
on emerging opportunities, understanding M&A best practices becomes
essential. This book will guide you through critical aspects of the
M&A process, from verifying land control to fostering collaboration
between teams.
Although the primary emphasis of this book is on mergers and
acquisitions, the expertise and practical insights and strategies
presented throughout are relevant across all stages of project
development. Each chapter provides best practices for navigating the
complexities of developing large-scale renewable projects. Whether you
are an industry veteran or new to the field, this book aims to provide
valuable insights into the complexities and nuances of acquiring and
developing renewable energy projects.

The renewable energy sector is evolving rapidly, with M&A
activities playing a pivotal role in shaping the industry’s future.
Whether you are an industry veteran or new to the field, this book aims
to provide valuable insights into the complexities and nuances of
acquiring and developing renewable energy projects.
As companies strive to meet ambitious pipeline goals and capitalize
on emerging opportunities, understanding M&A best practices becomes
essential. This book will guide you through critical aspects of the
M&A process, from verifying land control to fostering collaboration
between teams. We will address the following:
1. Introduction to M&A Trends in Renewable
Energy
We will explore the current surge in M&A activities within the
renewable energy sector. And we will explain why companies opt for
acquisitions over greenfield development and how this trend impacts
project timelines and market entry strategies.
2. The Critical First Step—Verifying Land
Control
We will explain why verifying land control is essential and detail
steps to confirm ownership and avoid legal issues.
3. Ensuring Correct Ownership and Signatories

including life estates and joint ownership. We will describe how to
Develop and implement strategies to verify the identification of all

4. Navigating Local Risks—Mineral Rights and
Beyond
We will examine regional risks that can affect project viability,
such as mineral rights issues and state-specific regulations. We will
provide insights on how to identify and mitigate these risks
effectively.
5. Effective Due Diligence Strategies Under Time
Constraints
You will learn strategies for conducting thorough due diligence
within tight M&A timelines. We will provide guidance on utilizing
existing documentation and identifying key areas that can improve
efficiency.
6. Environmental and Site Considerations
You will learn about assessing environmental factors that can impact
a project, such as floodplains and protected habitats. We will explain
how to incorporate these considerations into the M&A process using
public records and specialist input.
7. Unveiling Hidden Ownership Complexities
We will uncover the challenges posed by complex ownership structures
like life estates and trusts. And we will guide you on navigating these
complexities to ensure lease validity and project insurability.
8. Bridging the Gap—Collaboration Between Commercial and
Development Teams
Here we will address the potential friction between M&A teams and
development teams. You will learn strategies to enhance collaboration,
align objectives, and improve project outcomes.
9. Valuation and Timing—Assessing Project Worth
Accurately
In this section we will explore how due diligence findings and
project timing affect valuation. We will examine how to adjust
valuations based on risks to ensure accurate assessments aligned with
COD targets.
10. The Perils and Opportunities of Inheriting Existing
Projects
We will examine the challenges and benefits of inheriting projects
from other developers. Additionally, you will acquire strategies for
managing inherited tasks, utilizing established relationships, and
allocating resources efficiently.
Successful M&A comes from checking many boxes. Sometimes, it is
necessary to reject commercially promising projects if they exceed the
development team’s capabilities. Due diligence, collaboration, and
proactive risk management are essential for successful M&A
outcomes.

section: Riding the Wave - Current M&A Trends in Renewable Energy
text:
The renewable energy sector is experiencing a dynamic shift, with
mergers and acquisitions becoming a cornerstone strategy for growth and
expansion. This trend reflects the industry’s maturation and the
increasing complexity of developing large-scale renewable projects.
Why Companies Prefer M&A Over Greenfield Development
Greenfield development means beginning from the ground up, including
site selection, permitting, financing, and construction, which can take
years. In comparison, acquiring existing projects offers various
advantages:
Time Efficiency: Expedites operational readiness by
eliminating initial development phases. Risk Mitigation: Reduces exposure to development
risks like permitting delays or community opposition. Strategic Positioning: Allows companies to quickly
enter new markets or technologies. Resource Optimization: Enables better allocation of
resources by focusing on operational efficiency rather than development
hurdles.
Solar projects typically require five to seven years, while wind
projects can take seven to ten years, not including permitting on public
lands. Public lands can involve various stakeholders such as the Bureau
of Land Management, or the Bureau of Indian Affairs. The process of
securing land rights may be significantly prolonged when numerous
stakeholders are engaged.
M&A lets you skip the initial development phase, saving a great
deal of time and risk. An acquired project lets you avoid early-stage
uncertainties and achieve revenue sooner.
M&A Projects Span a Wide Spectrum of Development Stages
Pre-construction projects possess land leases and may have obtained
necessary permits; however, construction activities have not yet
commenced. Under-Construction Projects: Physical construction has started,
reducing uncertainty around project realization. Operational Projects: Already generating energy and revenue,
providing immediate cash flow.

Market Drivers Behind the M&A Surge
Regulatory Incentives: Policies like the Investment
Tax Credit (ITC) and Production Tax Credit (PTC) in the U.S. incentivize
timely project completion. Market Demand: Corporations and utilities are
increasing renewable energy procurement to meet sustainability
goals. Financial Markets: Low interest rates and high
liquidity make financing acquisitions more attractive. Technological Maturity: Advances in technology
reduce operational risks, making existing projects more valuable.

Industry Observations
At a recent conference, we participated in several discussions that
focused on M&A strategies. Many companies are now interested in
acquiring projects past the initial stage.
This reflects a strategic shift where companies aim to enhance their
portfolios quickly to meet market demands and investor expectations.
Understanding these trends is essential for stakeholders in the
renewable energy sector. Companies considering M&A must navigate
complex due diligence processes to ensure successful acquisitions.

title: Chapter 2: Verifying Land Control – The Foundation of Acquisition
section: Verifying Land Control – The Foundation of Acquisition
text:
Is the land you’re getting, really your land? In the realm of
renewable energy projects, land is a fundamental asset. Before
finalizing any acquisition, it’s imperative to verify land control and
access to ensure that the project rests on solid ground—literally and
legally.
Land control is the cornerstone of every successful renewable energy
project. It assures that a developer has the legal authority to enter,
use, and develop a specified plot of land for project development.
Without appropriate site supervision, even the most promising projects
might suffer major delays, legal battles, or catastrophic failure.
Critical Path Parcels
Developers should identify “critical path parcels” early in the
diligence process, including substations, transmission corridors, access
routes, collector systems, and key interconnection areas. Title defects
or site-control failures affecting these parcels can create
disproportionate impacts on financing, construction sequencing, and COD
schedules.
Critical Path Parcels Substations Transmission Corridors Access Routes Collector Systems Inter- connection Title defects here have disproportionate impact on financing & COD
Typically, renewable energy projects acquire property via leases,
easements, or purchase agreements to construct solar, wind, storage, or
transmission facilities. Land control ensures that the developer has the
right to build and run the project on the specified land, providing
stability and predictability throughout the project’s existence.
Developers should work closely with title companies and ALTA
surveyors to identify required Table A items and endorsement
requirements early in the transaction process. Optional survey
certifications frequently become mandatory lender or title requirements
during financing and closing.
Government Land Complexity and Overlapping Rights
Developers often assume that acquiring rights from a state or local
government agency will be more straightforward than negotiating with
private landowners. In practice, government-owned land can introduce an
entirely different layer of complexity into renewable energy
acquisitions.
State trust lands, public university lands, water districts,
county-owned property, and other public holdings frequently involve
overlapping interests that are not immediately visible during
preliminary diligence. A developer may secure a lease or development
agreement only to discover later that another party retains grazing
rights, farming rights, mineral interests, water access rights, or
operational easements affecting the same property. In some cases, these
third-party rights can directly interfere with substations, access
corridors, collector systems, or interconnection infrastructure.
Checkerboard Ownership
One of the most common mistakes developers make is assuming that site
control over one parcel automatically guarantees access across adjoining
parcels. In many Western states, renewable energy projects cross
“checkerboard” ownership patterns involving combinations of state,
federal, tribal, and private land. Each parcel may carry different
approval standards, title requirements, timelines, and regulatory
obligations. Legal access across one tract does not necessarily
establish access rights across the next.

Checkerboard Ownership Pattern Federal Private State Tribal Private Federal Tribal State Dashed line = one hypothetical project footprint Crosses Private, State, Federal & Tribal land — four separate approval processes
These layered ownership structures can create substantial transaction
risk if they are not identified early in the diligence process. Critical
path parcels, particularly those involving access roads, substations,
transmission corridors, or interconnection routes, should receive
heightened scrutiny whenever public land is involved.
Public vs. Private Sector Timelines
Developers should also recognize that public-sector transactions
frequently operate on timelines that are different from private
transactions. Many state and local agencies face staffing shortages,
outdated systems, and increasing development volume. Even after
commercial terms have been negotiated, agreements may require additional
review by agency counsel, governing boards, or state attorneys general
before execution can occur. Minor revisions to legal descriptions,
formatting, or access provisions can delay approvals for weeks or
months.
Because of these realities, successful renewable energy development
on government land requires more than simply following procedural
requirements. It requires proactive communication, relationship
management, and coordination across multiple stakeholders. Experienced
developers understand that resolving issues often depends on identifying
the right contacts within agencies, maintaining consistent
communication, and treating public-sector entities as long-term project
partners rather than transactional counterparties.
When government-owned parcels are involved, diligence must extend
beyond the lease itself. Developers should verify all existing rights
affecting the property, confirm legal access across adjoining tracts,
prioritize critical infrastructure parcels early, and build additional
time into acquisition and financing schedules to account for
administrative review processes. By approaching government land
strategically rather than reactively, developers can reduce transaction
delays, strengthen site control, and improve financing certainty.
Feasibility Studies
Land control is critical during the first feasibility studies and
project planning phases. Before a large-scale project can proceed,
developers must examine the land’s suitability, conduct environmental
assessments, and verify compliance with local legislation. These studies
cannot be conducted without site control, resulting in the project being
halted before it even begins.
Securing Financing
Lenders and investors want developers to demonstrate that they have
obtained land control before they can obtain financing for the project.
Having legal title to the land guarantees investors that the project has
a firm basis and will proceed without unanticipated legal issues.
Without land control, a project is considered high-risk, making it
extremely difficult to acquire funding.
Permits and Regulatory Compliance
Permitting processes for renewable energy projects frequently demand
verification of land control to proceed. Local zoning boards, regulatory
agencies, and environmental authorities may refuse to process permits
unless the developer can demonstrate that he or she owns or leases the
requisite land. Without land control, obtaining the required permits
becomes impossible.
Managing Risk
Acquiring land control early in the project’s lifespan allows
developers to prevent potential legal conflicts and delays. With good
land control, developers can proactively address potential concerns such
as land ownership conflicts, title issues, or community objections. This
lowers the likelihood of delays or project derailments later in the
development phase.
Protecting Project Timelines
Renewable energy projects are frequently time-sensitive, particularly
if they entail specific incentive schemes or financing deadlines. If
site control is not acquired early on, projects may encounter delays
that force them to miss critical deadlines, risking finance or incentive
eligibility.
Long-term land control agreements ensure that the developer has
ongoing access to the land to operate and maintain the projects. This is
especially crucial for wind and solar farms, whose infrastructure
requires frequent maintenance, repairs, and improvements.
The Significance of Land Verification
Failure to confirm land control can lead to:
Legal Disputes: Challenges from actual landowners
or third parties who hold interests in the land. Operational Delays: Inability to proceed with
development due to unresolved land or access issues. Financial Losses: Costs associated with litigation,
renegotiation of leases, or project cancellation.
Verifying land ownership and usage is essential to proactively
identify and address potential issues.
Case Study - Access Road We once worked on a storage project in Fallbrook, California. The
property was situated away from the main road and was not visible when
traveling on the frontage road. We believed that all the necessary
rights had been secured until we spoke with inspectors at the fire
department, who raised concerns due to the site’s location and its
distance from the main road. After inspection, the fire department
required a second access point at the back of the project. Since the
project was relatively near the frontage road, the developer did not
consider having to build a second access road. Securing agreements with
the landowners was now essential to the project’s development and
completion. Failing to confirm land usage rights can result in legal disputes
with landowners and stakeholders, which can cause unexpected delays and
financial losses. For our storage project, this entailed additional
expenses related to the design and the engineering of a second access
route. Relevant land use authorities must inspect even apparently
realistic access to confirm its insurability. You could drive from point
A to point B to reach the main road. Yet this project showed that it may
not be insurable due to unexpected fire department regulations. These
things must be considered when conducting due diligence for a
project.
Land Control & Ownership Disputes
One of the challenges that may arise is landowner disputes, which
account for 40% of potential issues that are encountered. As with the
storage project, this can seriously affect the project timeline. Are you
sure you own the land you believe you do? Review all agreements, as they
are vital to confirming ownership. Title ownership may be proven in
various ways. People can hold title and trust. They can hold titles and
own corporations. Sometimes, children inherit the property. I’ve spoken
with either a son or daughter and they say “Yes, I control everything.”
Although they may believe they’re on the title, records or deeds could
indicate that the property belongs to the parents. Understanding who has
authority over the property is critical.
Case Study - Clearing a Legacy Road Reservation to Ensure
Smooth Closing A historical municipal roadway reservation surfaced during title
review for a planned battery storage project. Through early diligence,
strong communication, and coordination between the developer,
municipality and title professionals, the issue was resolved well before
closing. Background A developer was advancing a battery storage project in Virginia when
a potential title issue surfaced during diligence. Historical records
showed that the local municipality had reserved the option to develop a
roadway through the property. Although the road had never been
constructed and the surrounding area had not developed as originally
envisioned, the reservation remained in the title record. Because the
proposed roadway alignment would have cut directly through the planned
battery storage site, the issue needed to be resolved before title
insurance could be issued without exception. Risk Identified Even though the roadway had never been built, the municipality
technically retained the right to construct it. If exercised, that right
could disrupt or even prevent the development of the battery storage
facility. For the developer and its investors, the presence of this
unresolved issue created uncertainty. From a title insurance
perspective, the insurer needed confirmation that the municipality no
longer intended to pursue the roadway before coverage could be
finalized. Strategy and Coordination Rather than waiting until the closing timeline became compressed, the
project team addressed the issue early. The developer, project manager,
legal counsel, title team, and closing team worked together to determine
what documentation would satisfy underwriting requirements. An important part of this process was the involvement of a
knowledgeable title insurance sales representative who had been working
with the client from the beginning of the project and understood both
the developer’s priorities and the underwriting requirements needed to
close the transaction. That relationship created an open line of
communication that allowed the parties to work through the issue
collaboratively rather than reactively. Multiple conversations were required to align expectations between
the developer, counsel, the title closer, and underwriting. Through
those discussions, the team clarified the specific language that would
be required from the municipality to satisfy underwriting requirements.
Once that guidance was clear, the developer engaged directly with the
appropriate municipal officials to request a letter confirming that the
municipality had no plans to construct the roadway. Working with the municipality demanded persistence and coordination.
The matter could not be resolved immediately because the process
involved procedural steps. Since the issue was identified months in
advance and the title sales representative kept it visible to the team,
the parties had enough time to work through it. Outcome The municipality ultimately provided the requested confirmation
letter stating that it did not intend to construct the roadway. With
that documentation in place, the title insurer was able to move forward
with coverage. Because the issue had been identified and addressed
early, the letter was secured several weeks before closing and the
transaction proceeded without delay. Key Takeaway Early diligence and proactive communication can prevent historical
land issues from becoming closing obstacles. Just as important is having
experienced title professionals involved throughout the process. A
knowledgeable title insurance sales representative who understands both
the development timeline and underwriting requirements can help
coordinate conversations, advocate for the client, and keep all parties
aligned while complex issues are being resolved. Case Study Submitted by Senior Title Insurance Expert Tara
Brown-Selders
Power of Attorney
A challenge we frequently encounter is power of attorney. Power of
attorney is often statutory in nature, requiring strict adherence to
relevant compliance regulations. There are important rules governing its
use, including specific protocols for signing documents. These things
will come up and details matter. During due diligence, some issues will
inevitably arise, particularly risks related to not confirming authority
and ownership. You may end up with invalid or unenforceable leases. You
may face delays, incur additional costs, have ownership disputes, and
litigation. Many issues can impact property and insurability.
Provide the title company with required documents such as a power of
attorney, trust certificate, or corporate records, so it can verify
authority to execute and enforce agreements. Small details also matter.
A different middle initial, such as George E. Smith versus George R.
Smith, may indicate two different people. This is especially important
when reviewing the chain of title. You should also confirm suffixes such
as Jr. and Sr. to ensure the correct parties are under contract.
Joint Tenancy, Trusts & Unrecorded Rights
Developers can be caught off guard by joint tenancy and trusts.
Unrecorded rights can be a huge problem. When examining a title, it is
common to assume that all information is documented. A significant
amount of information has been documented. We have occasionally
encountered challenges around unrecorded rights. It is important to have
a survey document or a checklist that is reviewed with the landowners.
The landowners will know whether there are capped wells, or whether
there has been mineral production on the property. They will know
whether the adjacent landowner uses their property to gain access to the
main road. They will also know whether there are conservation reserve
easements which can impact where and how you can develop.
You may have an area or a planned access route that you can drive on,
but it may not necessarily constitute a right that can be insured. And
when you take it to the title insurance company, they’re going to
require that you go out and perfect that. You may have to create
curative documents.
We have seen the time frames around title change and get longer.
Select a title company with expertise in ALTA coverage and renewable
energy projects. Work with a title company that can support a
transaction. While not all transactions reach a billion dollars, many
do. Many title carriers will have caps on how far and how much insurance
they can write. Establish those relationships early, being clear about
your project requirements is extremely important.
Farmlands & Unrecorded Rights
Something we often see is grazing and farming leases and water
rights. Pay attention to farming, because these are off record rights,
yet they are typically parties that have an interest in the land and
that will need to be addressed. While no immediate action may be
required for your M&A transaction, maintaining awareness of this
matter remains important. Illinois and some other jurisdictions have
laws specifying when notice must be given to farming tenants. It must be
provided by a specific date; if not, you’ll need to ensure compliance
through other means. If your project relies on starting construction in
January but you miss the November notification date, you may need to
adjust your figures.
The Wetlands Challenge
Developing projects on or near wetlands requires balancing energy
needs with the imperative to preserve biodiversity, water quality, and
the flood control functions wetlands provide. Wetlands pose significant
challenges to renewable energy development by requiring careful
management of potential ecological damage from construction and
operation, necessitating specialized building techniques for projects
like solar farms on piles, and involving complex regulatory frameworks
designed to protect these sensitive ecosystems. Projects must be
designed to achieve minimal disturbance to the wetland’s ecological
system, often involving compromises in design or location.
Habitat Disturbance
The construction and maintenance of renewable energy infrastructure,
such as solar panel foundations, can disturb wetland habitats and the
diverse plant and animal life they support. Wetlands are biologically
rich ecosystems, and energy projects could negatively impact various
species, requiring careful planning to minimize harm.
Regulation and Policy
Wetlands are often protected under various environmental regulations
(e.g., North American Wetlands Conservation Act) that govern their use
and limit development. Installing ground-mounted renewable energy
systems like solar panels on wetlands necessitates specialized piling
techniques to minimize ground disturbance and support the
infrastructure. While challenging to build on, the proximity of wetlands
to water bodies can sometimes reduce the length of electrical cabling,
potentially increasing power generation efficiency and lowering
costs.
Wetlands should be considered during site selection, design and
construction, because simple things can become big issues. Solar, wind,
and storage projects each face unique challenges that require
comprehensive planning beyond land rights.
Key Steps in Verifying Land Control
Cross-referencing leases and maps. Ensure that the geographical area represented in the map aligns with
the legal descriptions in lease agreements. Utilize Geographic Information Systems (GIS) to accurately map out
land parcels. Review vesting deeds. Obtain and examine the deeds that establish
current ownership. Identify any discrepancies between the deedholders and those who
have signed the leases.
Assess Title Documentation
Developers should recognize that title searches rely heavily on
public records, which may themselves be incomplete, inaccurate, or
outdated. If title review is rushed or based on insufficient
information, material defects such as liens, easements, restrictions, or
ownership discrepancies may be overlooked. These omissions can create
future insurability concerns, financing delays, and increased legal
exposure.
Check title reports for liens, encumbrances, or easements. Be aware
that in many cases, especially early-stage projects, full title work may
not have been conducted.
ALTA Surveys and Advanced Title Review: Protecting Site Control
In renewable energy acquisitions, site control is far more than a
signed lease or a marked parcel on a map. Sophisticated buyers, lenders,
tax equity investors, and title insurers increasingly expect developers
to demonstrate that the legal description of the project aligns
precisely with the physical realities on the ground. This is where ALTA
surveys and advanced title review become indispensable.
Too often, early-stage projects rely on outdated boundary sketches,
incomplete or limited title work prepared during preliminary
development. While these materials may appear sufficient during initial
negotiations, they frequently fail under the scrutiny of financing,
underwriting, or acquisition due diligence. Small discrepancies
discovered late in the transaction process can create outsized
consequences. A fence crossing a property line, an undefined access
route, an abandoned irrigation ditch, or an unrecorded utility easement
may seem minor at first glance, yet each can materially affect project
layout, financing certainty, insurability, and ultimately the ability to
close the transaction.
An ALTA survey provides the level of precision required for
utility-scale renewable energy projects. Unlike a basic boundary survey,
a full ALTA/NSPS Land Title Survey identifies visible encroachments,
access routes, rights-of-way, improvements, utility corridors, and
easements affecting the property. It establishes accurate monumentation
and provides lenders and title insurers with confidence that the legal
description reflected in leases, easements, and financing documents
accurately matches existing site conditions.
Every Agreement Depends on Survey Accuracy
For renewable energy transactions, survey precision is critical
because every downstream agreement depends upon it. Interconnection
corridors, collector lines, substations, battery storage locations,
turbine setbacks, and access roads all rely upon accurate legal
descriptions. If the survey reveals inconsistencies after financing
documents have already been drafted, developers may face expensive
curative work, redesign costs, delayed financial closings, or even
threats to tax-credit qualification timelines.
Tier-1 ALTA Surveys
Developers should also recognize that not all ALTA surveys provide
the same level of protection. Many lenders and institutional investors
now require full Tier-1 ALTA surveys with extended coverage and
lender-specific certifications. These surveys provide greater detail
regarding improvements, visible easements, encroachments, and access
conditions. Attempts to reduce costs through limited survey products
frequently shift risk downstream into the financing and closing process,
where remediation becomes significantly more expensive and time
sensitive.
Equally important is the relationship between the ALTA survey and the
title commitment. A survey alone cannot identify all project risks.
Advanced title review is necessary to uncover recorded and off-record
matters that may interfere with development or financing. This review
often extends far beyond the current ownership deed and requires
examination of historical conveyances, easements, restrictions,
mortgages, rights-of-way, and prior reservations affecting the
property.
In many renewable energy projects, some of the most significant risks
are not immediately visible in public records. Neighbor access
arrangements, oral farming leases, historical roadway reservations,
irrigation rights, unrecorded utility agreements, conservation
restrictions, and legacy covenants can all create substantial project
complications if left unresolved. Developers who fail to investigate
these issues early may discover them only during financing diligence or
immediately before closing, when timelines are compressed and leverage
is reduced.
Comprehensive title review also requires careful evaluation of title
commitment exceptions. Blanket easements, undefined utility corridors,
vague access rights, and historical reservations often conceal
operational risks that may later interfere with construction or
long-term operations. Experienced development teams work closely with
title counsel, surveyors, and underwriters to clarify exceptions,
negotiate coverage enhancements, and obtain accurate exhibits that
define the precise location of third-party rights. This may involve
boundary line agreements, easement relocations, subordination
agreements, corrective deeds, or escrow arrangements designed to manage
unresolved risks while preserving transaction timelines.
Ultimately, ALTA surveys and advanced title review are foundational
risk-management tools that protect site control, support project
finance, improve insurability, and strengthen acquisition certainty. In
an industry where project value depends heavily on execution timing and
bankability, thorough survey and title diligence can mean the difference
between a successful closing and a delayed or failed transaction.
Unresolved Defects Impact Valuation & Financing
Successful renewable energy acquisitions increasingly depend upon
proactive title curative strategies. Developers should identify title
defects early, prioritize issues affecting
Understanding Lease Terms
Evaluate the duration, renewal options, and any conditions that
might affect long-term project viability. Ensure that the leases are financeable and meet the requirements of
lenders and investors.
Challenges in Land Verification
Incomplete Documentation: Early-stage projects
might not have comprehensive land records. Time Constraints: Tight M&A timelines may limit
the depth of verification possible. Complex Ownership Structures: Land may be owned by
multiple parties or entities, complicating verification.
Best Practices
Engage Land Specialists: Professionals with
experience in land acquisition and title review can identify issues that
might be overlooked. Utilize Public Records: Access county records,
property tax records, and other public databases to supplement provided
documentation. Prioritize Critical Parcels: Focus on key areas
essential for project infrastructure, such as substation sites or main
access points.
Securing land control is a critical phase in the development of a
renewable energy project. It establishes the legal framework that
enables developers to plan, finance, and execute projects without undue
delay or danger. By addressing land control early on and adhering to
best practices, developers can create the framework for a successful
project. Verifying land control is not just a formality but a critical
step that safeguards the investment and ensures that the project’s
foundation is secure.

title: Chapter 3: Ensuring Correct Ownership – Getting the Signatures Right
section: Ensuring Correct Ownership – Getting the Signatures Right
text:
Before a renewable energy project can be built, developers must
secure legal rights to use the land. This includes leases, purchase
options, and access agreements. However, delays or gaps in site control
can stall the project and alarm investors. Securing valid agreements
hinges on obtaining signatures from all rightful owners of the land.
Overlooking ownership complexities can render leases unenforceable and
introduce significant risks. Ownership verification is critical. Have
the right people signed? Have you reviewed deeds? Has title search been
completed?
During early development or when reviewing a project for a merger or
acquisition, it is important to be aware of five common mistakes:
Five Common Signature Mistakes 1. Assuming legal access exists without a deeded easement 2. Not verifying ownership across the entire site 3. Skipping the title commitment review 4. Letting land agreements sit without updates 5. Assuming curative work can wait
1. Assuming Legal Access Exists
A road shown on a map does not guarantee legal access. Easements may
be missing, expired, or simply not recorded. Check to see whether there
is a deeded easement. If the project relies on verbal agreements,
historical arrangements, or goodwill, it is at risk. Prioritize key
areas essential for project infrastructure or main access points.
Confirm legal access for all parcels; identify and record necessary
easements.
2. Not Verifying Ownership Across the Entire Site
Multiple individuals can share ownership. This is particularly common
with large or inherited family lands. Even worse, records may not
reflect recent changes like deaths, trusts, or quitclaims. If an owner
is missing from a signature block, the lease or option might not be
valid. Initiate curative work to identify and resolve ownership
discrepancies, outdated instruments, and missing interests. Engaging
land specialists can expedite this process.
3. Skipping the Title Commitment Review
The title commitment is an important document. This is where red
flags hide: mineral rights carve-outs, old mortgages, utility easements,
or overlapping rights from past deals. These are frequently overlooked
deal breakers. Order and review title commitments, identifying
exceptions related to mineral leases, water rights, environmental laws,
or cultural heritage sites.
4. Letting Land Agreements Sit Without Updates
Did you sign a letter of intent or option years ago? Expired,
incorrect, or missing land parcels need renegotiation. Your agreement is
only as strong as its paper trail and expiration clause. Align ALTA
survey boundaries with title and landowner agreements. Cross reference
leases and maps with legal descriptions in lease agreements. Ensure that
all site control documents are valid, assignable, and fully
executed.
5. Assuming Curative Work Can Wait
Curative work takes time. If you wait to fix gaps in ownership,
access, or title, it’s often too late. Probate, corporate consents, and
lien releases can take months. We’ve witnessed renewable energy projects
stopped in their tracks due to unforeseen legal challenges related to
the land. Title Curative is an essential part of the process when it
comes to large-scale renewable energy projects. It includes securing
necessary consents, subordinations, and crossing permits to achieve
successful project financing. Research deed documents and conduct
boundary surveys to obtain accurate title and legal description
information, ensuring you can proceed confidently. Start early,
everything takes longer than you think.
Curative Is a Relay Race
Title curative is rarely a one-time exercise. It requires ongoing
coordination among land teams, surveyors, legal counsel, title
underwriters, lenders, and developers. Successful projects establish
clear communication channels, assign ownership responsibility early, and
maintain structured follow-up processes to ensure defects are resolved
before financing deadlines.
Title Curative Is the Linchpin of Financing
Title curative is a transaction-management discipline. Financing
timelines drive curative urgency. Title curative is often the linchpin
of a successful financing close. Systematically identifying defects,
prioritizing cures, coordinating stakeholders, and managing residual
exposure through escrows and endorsements can materially reduce
transaction delays and improve financing certainty.
Title Curative Is a Relay Race Land Team Surveyor Legal Counsel Title Underwriter Lender / Close
Common Ownership Complexities
Life Estates: A life estate grants an individual
rights to a property for their lifetime. Example: A property deeded to
Mr. and Mrs. Smith with a reservation that Grandma retains a life
estate. Implication: If Grandma hasn’t signed the lease, the agreement
is incomplete and not insurable. Joint Tenancy and Tenancy in Common: Properties
owned by multiple individuals, each with equal or proportionate shares.
All owners must consent and sign agreements for them to be valid. Trusts and Corporate Entities: Properties held in
trusts or by corporations require signatures from authorized
representatives. Verification of authority is essential. Unrecorded Interests: Rights or claims not
reflected in public records, such as verbal agreements or unrecorded
easements.
Strategies for Ensuring Correct Ownership and Signatories
Conduct Thorough Title Searches: Identify all
current owners and their respective interests. Review for any
reservations, easements, liens, or other encumbrances. Review Vesting Deeds in Detail: Check vesting deeds
and title history for irregularities. Pay attention to reservations like
life estates or mineral rights. Verify Authority of Signatories: Ensure that
individuals signing on behalf of entities have the legal authority to do
so. Obtain corporate resolutions or trustee certifications when
necessary. Consult Legal Experts: Engage attorneys
specializing in real estate and energy transactions. Address complex
scenarios proactively. Potential Risks of Neglecting Ownership
Verification: Invalid leases, agreements may be deemed
unenforceable, affecting project legality. Delays and Added Costs: Time and money spent
resolving ownership disputes. Insurability Issues: Title insurance may not cover
leases with incomplete ownership consent.
Case Study – Life Estates In one instance, a developer failed to recognize that a life estate
holder had not signed the lease. When the oversight was discovered
during the financing phase, the project faced significant delays as the
developer had to renegotiate with the life estate holder, who then
demanded more favorable terms. During a recent closing, it was necessary to obtain signed lease
amendments from all landowners involved. Learning that one woman’s
health was failing, we prioritized her signing of the amendment so it
could be recorded quickly. She passed away the day after signing, just
as we were recording the amendment. She had 13 heirs who would have had
to sign any subsequent documents. We were grateful to our community for
helping us gain this insight and react quickly. Waiting would have
postponed the closing for weeks due to probate and identifying and
locating the heirs. We have an issue right now with a project where the mother is
incapacitated and her daughter will potentially sign in two capacities —
as her successor under a trust, and under a power of attorney, each
document having their own unique issues. To have the daughter sign for
the trust we need the physician’s letter in compliance with HIPAA and
the terms of the trust, confirming the mother’s incapacity. In such
cases, the power of attorney must be durable and authorize real estate
transactions. Signing in Two Capacities for an Incapacitated Owner Daughter, signing on mother's behalf Daughter, signing on mother's behalf As Trust Successor Requires: physician's letter (HIPAA-compliant) confirming incapacity, consistent with the trust's own terms Under Power of Attorney Requires: POA must be durable (survives incapacity) and specifically authorize real estate transactions
Conclusion
Ensuring that all rightful owners have signed agreements is not just
a legal necessity but a cornerstone of project security and
bankability.
Ownership Scenarios & Required Signatories Sole Ownership 1 deed holder ✓ Confirm identity ✓ Match deed name to signature Joint Tenancy / Tenancy in Common All co-owners ✓ Every owner signs ✓ Confirm % shares Life Estate Life tenant + Remainderman ✓ Life tenant signs ✓ Document remainder interest Trust / Entity Trustee or corporate officer ✓ Verify authority ✓ Trustee cert. / corp. resolution

sole ownership, joint tenancy, life estate) with checklists of steps to
ensure valid agreements are in place for each type.
