title: Chapter 4: Unseen Challenges - Navigating Mineral Rights
text:
When acquiring land, it is important to understand that there are
surface rights and there are severed rights; rights that are separate
from surface ownership. Mineral rights refer to ownership of underground
minerals. Subsurface severances refer to minerals or the subsurface
estate that is legally separated from the surface estate. Because
mineral rights laws vary significantly by jurisdiction, developers
should consult qualified legal counsel and title professionals regarding
project-specific risks and compliance obligations.
In many states, mineral rights can be separated from surface rights,
allowing different owners for underground resources and the land above.
The mineral owner typically has the dominant estate, which means that
they have the right to access the surface to extract minerals.
Tribal Mineral Rights Complexity
On tribal lands the federal government may own the subsurface estate,
while private individuals or tribes own the surface. This is typically
set for a fixed term, after which mineral rights return to the surface
owner. This is also called term mineral interests. This is most common
in Texas and other U.S. states with complex oil and gas laws.
Mineral rights on tribal lands may also involve separate federal
oversight, or distinct tribal governance requirements. Surface and
subsurface rights are not always aligned, and additional approvals may
be required before development can proceed. These complexities can
materially affect title insurability, financing certainty, and project
timelines.
Developers should approach tribal projects as long-term
government-to-government relationships rather than conventional land
acquisitions. Successful projects depend as much on trust, transparency,
and cultural understanding as they do on contractual structure and
financing execution.
From Severance to Curative: Why Mineral Rights Demand Specialized
Due Diligence
Mineral Ownership Report (MOR) Pathway Order MOR Flag severance early Historical title research Heirship / chain reconstruction Curative waivers / subordination Insurable
When minerals are severed from the surface estate, the property
instantly has two chains of title: one for the surface and one for the
subsurface. While the surface chain can usually be reviewed by a title
company, the subsurface requires a specialized search – known as a
Mineral Ownership Report (MOR).
Unlike a standard title commitment, an MOR often traces ownership
back to the 1800s.
Why an MOR Looks Back 150+ Years ~1880s Original severance deed recorded Decades pass Heirs inherit rights they don't know exist No production Rights sit dormant, records go stale Today Renewable project needs an MOR
This complexity stems from heirs inheriting rights they may not know
exist, forgotten leases, or rights never exercised until energy prices
made them valuable. As a result, developers can encounter “breaks” in
the chain, where ownership is unclear or fragmented across generations.
For M&A due diligence, the implications are profound:
Time – These searches can take months, making early
detection critical. Cost – Curative work to resolve gaps, probate
issues, or missing heirs can run high. Insurability – Subsurface rights must be
affirmatively insured just like surface rights, or deals risk collapse
at closing.
In some cases, prior production or exploration activity helps, since
oil and gas companies may have already conducted ownership research. But
where no production exists, developers must brace for lengthy
investigations.
Key M&A Takeaway: If a potential severance is
flagged, order MORs immediately. Ignoring subsurface rights until late
in the deal often results in closing delays, renegotiations, or failed
transactions.
Implications for Renewable Energy Projects
Surface Disruption: Holders of mineral rights are
typically entitled to access and utilize the land’s surface for the
purpose of mineral extraction. Operational Risks: Drilling or mining operations
may disrupt the functioning of renewable energy facilities. Insurance Limitations: Title insurance policies may
exclude coverage for mineral rights issues, thus increasing risk.
Operational Interference Risk
Mineral risks do not disappear simply because production is inactive
at the time of acquisition. Existing mineral owners may retain rights to
future surface access, pipelines, drilling pads, or production
infrastructure that could interfere with renewable operations years or
even decades after project construction.
Legal complexities differ substantially from one state to another,
presenting distinct challenges depending on the jurisdiction. These
rights can significantly impact land development.
Mineral Rights and Government Reservations
The significance of mineral rights is evident when we consider
projects such as solar installations, where costly equipment is placed
directly on the land’s surface.
It is essential to be aware that the government reserves mineral
rights on land grant deeds west of the Mississippi, often superseding
private ownership.
Implications for Developers
To protect your development interests, delve into the specifics of
land deeds and government reservations, as these can significantly
influence land use and access rights.
Mineral Rights and Extractions
While the U.S. government possesses the right to extract minerals
from private lands, it rarely exercises this right. Mineral resources
are broadly categorized into oil, gas, and coal, each with its own legal
rights and associated risks. It’s also vital to understand the
difference between shallow and deep rights in a vertical well, as the
resources accessible at different depths can vary significantly.
Implications for Developers
Developers must have a profound understanding of the specific mineral
categories in their project areas, as well as the associated rights and
risks. Detailed knowledge of well depths is crucial when planning
projects.
Mineral Rights and Regulations
There may be questions regarding the federal government’s authority
over mineral rights in Western states. While the answers vary, it’s
clear that private entities can lease these rights without requiring
government approval. The potential for conflicts arises when sourcing
minerals in areas where others are already engaged in mineral
extraction, known as “fracking.” Obtaining the necessary rights through
deeds or leases is crucial for any mining project.
Implications for Developers
To avoid disputes and legal entanglements, developers must navigate
the legal and regulatory framework surrounding mineral rights, including
royalty interests and ancillary interests that may impact the
project.
Mineral Rights’ Impact on Land Development
Mineral rights holders have the unique ability to access the entire
property without permission, including for oil and gas exploration,
which can significantly affect surface land use. Developers must
acknowledge the complexity of federal issues in the energy sector,
especially in solar and wind projects. It is imperative to assess the
specific risks associated with each project, including the value of
high-tech equipment and potential surface subsidence.
Implications for Developers
A comprehensive evaluation of the effects of mineral rights on land
development is essential, with an emphasis on anticipating and
mitigating potential challenges and risks.
Mineral Rights, Ownership, and Valuation
Texas takes a distinctive approach to mineral rights ownership,
setting aside areas for drilling pads and compelling mineral companies
to consent. Original land grants from Spain and England have a lasting
impact on property rights, particularly in southern Colorado.
Determining the value of mineral rights is a complex process that
involves multiple stakeholders, including title companies, oil and gas
engineers, and outside counsel. This process necessitates the
examination of mineral reports, lease validation, and expert opinions.
Importantly, the value of mineral rights is state-specific and not
regulated by the federal government. State-specific considerations
include:
Private Ownership States
Texas, Oklahoma, Pennsylvania, North Dakota: Minerals dominant over
surface.
Government Retention States
Colorado, New Mexico, Nevada, Arizona: Bureau of Land Management
oversight, disclosure states. Texas, Colorado, Montana, California: Mineral reservation disclosure
laws.
Dormant Rights States
Ohio, North Dakota, Indiana, Michigan, Pennsylvania: Dormant mineral
reversion laws.
Implications for Developers
To make informed decisions and navigate the complexities of mineral
rights, developers should become familiar with the processes for
determining their value and engage with experts to address these
intricate challenges.
Identifying Mineral Rights Risks
Conduct state-specific research, laws pertaining to mineral rights
vary by state. States like Oklahoma and Texas have active mineral
extraction industries with frequent mineral severances.
Flag Problem Areas: agricultural land with drilling
history, recent lease activity, or corporate mineral ownership. Title Examination: Review title commitments for
exceptions related to mineral rights. Identify any recorded mineral
leases, reservations, or severances for 75+ years. Landowner Engagement: Landowners may have knowledge
of mineral activities on their property. Ask about past or current
mineral leases or exploration activities. Public Records Search: Access county clerk records
and state mineral registries. Consult geological surveys and energy
department databases.
Why Mineral Rights Matter in Renewable Energy Development
When surface and subsurface rights split, everything changes. What
appears to be a straightforward title search can quickly become a
multi-year puzzle involving heirs no one knew existed, deeds recorded in
the 1800s, and ownership interests that do not appear in county records.
For developers and investors, that can mean one thing: risk.
At the core of many mineral rights issues is the concept of
severance. Types of mineral severances include:
Royalty Interests (NPRI & ORRI) Leasehold/Working Interests Split Estates Term Severances Fee Simple Severances
Severance occurs when the rights to minerals beneath the surface are
legally separated from the surface rights themselves. From that point
forward, the property no longer has a single clean chain of title.
Instead, there are two separate ownership histories:
Surface Chain of Title: The ownership history
typically identified through a standard title search conducted through
county records. Subsurface Chain of Title: A separate ownership
history governing the mineral estate beneath the property.
This distinction is critical because renewable energy developers are
often focused on surface use, while mineral owners may retain legal
rights to access and utilize the same property for extraction
activities.
Why Two Chains of Title Matter
Without severance, there is generally one chain of title, one
ownership review, and one title commitment from the title company. With
severance, developers may face:
Two separate chains of title Multiple ownership interests Additional title review requirements Separate risk mitigation obligations
This can create substantial complications, including:
Title insurance gaps Financing delays Access conflicts Increased legal and curative costs
The Role of a Mineral Ownership Report (MOR)
Mineral Ownership Reports (MORs) should be ordered early in the
diligence process, particularly in jurisdictions with historical oil and
gas activity or known severances. MOR preparation may require extensive
historical title analysis and coordination with specialized vendors.
Delayed mineral review can materially impact underwriting timelines,
financing certainty, and project closing schedules.
A Mineral Ownership Report (MOR) functions as a parallel title search
for the subsurface estate. It traces the chain of mineral ownership,
often back to the original severance deed, which in some regions may
date back more than 150 years. Without an MOR, developers may not fully
understand who controls the mineral estate beneath the project.
Challenges in Subsurface Ownership
Mineral ownership chains are often far more difficult to trace than
surface ownership due to:
Poor historical recordkeeping Generational inheritance gaps Gaps in the title chain Off-record agreements and undocumented transfers
Production vs. Dormant Rights
Dormant vs. Producing Mineral Rights Dormant No production history Records often incomplete Heirs hard to locate Risk = uncertainty Needs reconstruction Producing Active leases / operators Easier to trace ownership Mineral estate often dominant Risk = operational conflict Needs negotiation
Not all severed mineral estates present the same level of risk.
Dormant mineral rights are often harder to trace because ownership
records may not have been updated for decades. These situations
frequently require extensive historical research.
Actively producing mineral rights may be easier to identify due to
ongoing operations and recorded leases, but they often involve existing
contractual obligations and active operators, creating separate
negotiation challenges.
When Mineral Activity Changes the Risk Profile
Not all mineral rights create the same level of risk. Understanding
whether mineral rights are dormant, historically active, or currently
producing can dramatically alter the due diligence strategy, financing
timeline, project layout, and overall transaction risk profile.
One of the most important questions developers should ask during
early diligence is deceptively simple: “Has there ever been production
on this property, or even an attempt to produce?” The answer frequently
changes the entire trajectory of the transaction.
When no production has occurred, mineral ownership is often poorly
documented, fragmented across generations, or forgotten entirely.
Dormant mineral estates may appear harmless because no active drilling
or extraction is taking place, but dormant does not mean extinguished.
In many cases, these rights remain fully enforceable despite decades of
inactivity. Developers often discover that ownership records are
incomplete, heirs cannot easily be located, or interests have been
divided among numerous descendants through inheritance. Reconstructing
those ownership chains can require extensive curative work, including
probate review, heirship verification, and historical title analysis
stretching back generations.
Dormant mineral rights therefore create a different type of risk than
active production. The challenge is uncertainty. Developers may not know
who owns the rights, who has authority to execute agreements, or whether
additional claims may surface later during financing or construction.
Resolving those uncertainties often takes months and can materially
affect transaction timelines, financing certainty, and title
insurability.
Producing Mineral Rights
Producing mineral rights creates an entirely different category of
exposure. When minerals are actively being produced, or when active
leases remain in place, ownership is often easier to trace because oil
and gas operators have already conducted substantial research into the
mineral estate. Existing leases, royalty payments, production records,
and operator files may provide developers with a clearer picture of
ownership and activity.
Active production introduces operational conflicts that can directly
interfere with renewable energy development. In many jurisdictions, the
mineral estate is considered dominant over the surface estate, meaning
mineral owners or operators may retain broad rights to access and use
the surface as reasonably necessary for extraction activities. This can
create substantial complications for solar arrays, wind turbine
placement, battery storage infrastructure, access roads, collector
systems, and transmission corridors.
The degree of risk depends heavily on the type and status of
production activity. Historical production from abandoned or capped
wells may present lingering legal issues if leases were never formally
terminated or released. Active production creates ongoing surface-use
conflicts that frequently require negotiation of surface use waivers,
subordination agreements, or non-disturbance arrangements. Exploration
leases present another challenge because drilling may not yet have
begun, but operators retain the right to initiate future activity that
could disrupt project construction or operations.
For developers and investors, this distinction between dormant and
producing mineral estates is critical because each requires a different
mitigation strategy. Dormant rights demand extensive ownership
reconstruction and curative analysis. Active rights require negotiation,
operational coordination, and long-term risk management.
Comprehensive due diligence should therefore include a detailed
review of production history, lease activity, operator records, and
publicly available oil and gas databases. Developers should determine
whether production ever occurred, whether leases remain active, whether
surface use agreements exist, and whether any exploration activity or
permit filings suggest future development interest. These findings
directly influence project valuation, title underwriting, financing
terms, and construction planning.
Production status also plays a major role in title insurance and
lender risk analysis. Title insurers often evaluate active and
historical mineral activity much more closely than dormant estates
because producing properties carry a greater likelihood of operational
conflict. Underwriters may require recorded surface use waivers,
subordinations, or additional curative measures before issuing
affirmative coverage. In some cases, mineral-related risks may be
excluded from coverage if adequate protection cannot be secured.
Timing Is Critical
The timing of this analysis is equally important. One of the most
common mistakes in renewable energy acquisitions is waiting too long to
investigate production activity and mineral exposure. Mineral ownership
research, negotiations with operators, and curative work can take months
to complete. Projects that identify these risks early maintain far
greater flexibility to redesign layouts, negotiate agreements, adjust
valuation assumptions, or sequence financing accordingly.
In some cases, production activity can actually accelerate the
diligence process. Existing operators may already possess current
ownership records, established communication channels with mineral
holders, and documented surface agreements that simplify negotiations.
When approached proactively, operators can sometimes become valuable
partners in resolving mineral-related risks rather than obstacles to
development.
Ultimately, the distinction between dormant and producing mineral
rights is not simply a legal technicality. It is a core transaction
issue that affects project bankability, financing certainty, title
insurability, construction timing, and long-term operational stability.
Understanding that distinction early allows developers, lenders, and
investors to approach renewable energy acquisitions with a more
realistic assessment of risk and a stronger strategy for successful
execution.
The Impact on Project Development
Mineral rights can create three major categories of risk for
renewable energy projects:
Legal Risk Operational Risk Financial Risk
These risks can affect project layout, financing, insurability,
construction timing, and long-term operations.
Blanket Approaches Fail
Developers should not assume that mineral mitigation strategies are
uniform across all project types or jurisdictions. Utility-scale solar,
battery storage, transmission, and wind projects each present different
operational risks and surface-use considerations. Effective mitigation
requires a project-specific analysis that accounts for footprint,
infrastructure placement, future operational flexibility, and the
likelihood of mineral development activity.
Why Timing Is Critical
One of the most common mistakes developers make is waiting too long
to order Mineral Ownership Reports. Mineral ownership research can take
months. Negotiating waivers, subordinations, or surface use agreements
may take even longer. Early identification of mineral severances gives
project teams more flexibility to evaluate alternatives and resolve
conflicts before they threaten project timelines.
Best practices include:
Flagging severances early Ordering MORs quickly Engaging experienced mineral rights specialists Negotiating surface use waivers Planning for subordination agreements Building additional time into project schedules for curative
work
Beyond Mineral Rights—Other Regional Risks
Water Rights: Especially in arid regions, water
rights can be critical. Environmental Regulations: Local environmental laws
may impose additional requirements. Cultural Heritage Sites: Presence of indigenous
sites or historical landmarks can restrict development.
Mitigation Strategies
Early Due Diligence: Screen land early, conduct
thorough title review and mineral risk checks. Order a Mineral Ownership Report (MOR). Identify any active leases
or recorded permits. Review public records for existing oil/gas leases.
Investigate nearby permit filings. Review Site Geology: Assess the likelihood of
future mineral development. Obtain Surface Use Waivers: Agreements from mineral
rights holders not to disturb the surface. Secure Subordination Agreements: Mineral rights
owners agree that their interests are subordinate to the project’s
interests. Adjust Project Design: Avoid areas with significant
mineral rights activity.
Real-World Example
A solar project in Texas was delayed when oil drilling commenced on
the site. This was due to pre-existing mineral rights that were not
identified during due diligence. The developer ultimately entered
negotiations with the mineral rights owner, this resulted in a complete
project redesign, significant delays and increased costs.
Title Insurance and Risk Management
Mineral rights are not simply a land management issue. They directly
impact project finance and long-term bankability. Lenders, tax equity
investors, and future acquirers increasingly require developers to
identify and mitigate mineral risks before financing can proceed. Title
insurance plays a crucial role in protecting developers and lenders from
issues that could negatively affect their interests. Standard title
insurance policies frequently exclude mineral-related risks unless
specialized endorsements or a separate mineral ownership analysis is
obtained.
Some developers may mistakenly believe that a lack of mineral value
equates to no risk in mineral rights. However, this is far from the
truth. The risk of others claiming valuable minerals is a real concern.
It’s important to thoroughly research surface waiver agreements and
engage specialized title companies to prepare mineral ownership reports
that can de-risk minerals for title insurance.
Mineral Rights are a Bankability Trigger
Mineral rights are not simply a title issue; they are a bankability
issue. Lenders, tax equity investors, and future acquirers increasingly
require developers to identify and mitigate mineral risks before
financing can proceed. Standard title insurance policies often exclude
mineral-related risks unless specialized endorsements, curative actions,
or separate mineral ownership analysis are obtained. Even projects
financed on balance sheet may face future transaction challenges if
mineral exposure remains unresolved.
Implications for Developers
Understanding the nuances of title insurance is essential. Developers
must secure comprehensive coverage, consider endorsements to cover
mineral rights, and be prepared for the possibility of coverage denials
based on property owners’ legal rights. Collaborate with specialized
title companies that can provide comprehensive mineral rights
reports.
Surface Waivers for Solar Projects
Obtaining surface waivers for mineral rights can be challenging due
to the high threshold for signing and the potential need for monetary
compensation. Historical severances of mineral rights, predating modern
technology, can complicate surface area access.
Implications for Developers
Be prepared for challenges when negotiating surface waivers, and
consider alternatives, such as affidavits of non-production.
Case Study - Rethinking Mineral Surface Waiver
Requirements A battery energy storage system (BESS) project in Texas presented an
opportunity to evaluate mineral risk differently than traditional solar
development. By applying a project-specific analysis and facilitating
collaboration between the developer, title professionals, and
underwriting counsel, the parties structured a practical solution that
reduced curative work while maintaining insurability. Background Mineral rights present a common challenge in renewable energy
development across Texas. For solar projects, developers typically
obtain surface waivers from 100 percent of mineral owners to prevent
drilling or mineral development from interfering with solar arrays and
infrastructure. A battery storage project presented a different scenario. The
development site consisted of approximately thirty acres, but the
battery storage equipment would occupy only ten acres of the
property. Risk Identified The standard approach would have required obtaining surface waivers
from all mineral interest holders across the entire property. While
common for solar projects, that level of curative work can be costly and
time consuming. However, in this case the project design left a substantial portion
of the property unused. If mineral development were ever pursued, there
was sufficient land outside the battery storage footprint to accommodate
drilling activity without interfering with the project. Strategy and Coordination Recognizing the unique characteristics of battery storage
development, the project team evaluated whether a more practical
risk-based approach could be applied. The developer believed that obtaining surface waivers only across the
portion of the property where the battery storage equipment would be
located could sufficiently address the operational risk. Rather than
immediately defaulting to the traditional approach, the developer relied
on a trusted title insurance sales representative to help present the
concept to the title team and underwriting. That representative played a key role in facilitating discussions
between the developer, the closing team, and underwriting counsel.
Multiple conversations were required to review the site plan, the
acreage being utilized for the project, and the remaining land that
would still be available if mineral development ever occurred. Because renewable energy projects increasingly involve new
technologies and development patterns, the parties ultimately evaluated
the issue through a project specific lens rather than relying solely on
standard practice. After reviewing the project layout and risk profile, the team agreed
that surface waivers would only need to be obtained from mineral
interest holders covering approximately thirty percent of the property
rather than the entire acreage. Throughout the process, the sales representative continued to
advocate for the client while ensuring the title team and underwriter
were comfortable with the risk analysis and documentation required for
coverage. Outcome By tailoring the curative requirements to the specific project
footprint, the developer avoided unnecessary time and expense while
still satisfying underwriting requirements. The project was able to move
forward with appropriate title coverage while maintaining operational
flexibility across the remainder of the property. Key Takeaway Renewable energy development continues to introduce new project types
and land use patterns. Applying a thoughtful, project specific analysis
to mineral risks can create practical solutions that protect both the
developer and the title insurer while avoiding unnecessary curative
work. Equally important is the role of experienced title professionals who
understand both the development process and the underwriting
perspective. A trusted sales representative can help bridge those
perspectives, advocate for practical solutions, and facilitate the
communication necessary to move complex renewable energy transactions
forward. Case Study Submitted by Senior Title Insurance Expert Tara
Brown-Selders
Conclusion
Conflicts may occur when a renewable energy project necessitates the
use of surface land where mineral rights have previously been severed.
Mineral rights typically hold legal precedence over surface rights,
thereby allowing mineral owners the authority to access and utilize the
surface for resource extraction. To resolve this, renewable energy
developers must conduct thorough title research to identify mineral
ownership, engage in complex negotiations with mineral rights holders,
secure waivers or surface use agreements, and acquire specialized title
insurance to mitigate risks and protect their investment.
State laws differ in their treatment of mineral and surface rights,
so conducting due diligence and consulting state-specific legal
professionals is important for project planning. There is no
one-size-fits-all approach.

title: Chapter 5: Racing the Clock – Due Diligence Strategies for Tight Timelines
section: Racing the Clock – Due Diligence Strategies for Tight Timelines
text:
In the fast-paced world of mergers and acquisitions, companies often
face tight deadlines to complete critical due diligence. It’s important
to be thorough but efficient to ensure that no key issues are not
overlooked. Typically, M&A transactions allow for a 60 to 90-day
window for due diligence. Often, it is only a 60-day window, so you must
do a quick analysis to understand what needs to be done.
In accelerated transaction environments, projects with organized
documentation, clear site control, completed diligence, and
well-structured data rooms often command greater market interest and
move through financing and acquisition processes more efficiently than
less-prepared assets. Pipeline prioritization is critical.
Data Room Readiness
A Typical 60-Day Diligence Window Days 1–10: Data room audit Days 10–30: Title / survey / MOR Days 30–50: Curative & engagement Days 50–60: Close-out checklist Triage, not a slower 9-month process
A Typical 60-Day Diligence Window Days 1–10 Data room audit Days 10–30 Title / survey / MOR Days 30–50 Curative & engagement Days 50–60 Close-out checklist Triage, not a slower 9-month process
Well-organized data rooms containing current title materials,
surveys, permits, leases, environmental reports, and financing
documentation can significantly accelerate acquisition review and
improve buyer confidence during compressed transaction timelines.
An energy company successfully completed due diligence within a
60-day window by prioritizing critical leases and utilizing a
specialized team to focus on high-risk areas, thereby avoiding potential
delays in project development.
“Pre-Mortem” Risk Analysis
Some development teams conduct “pre-mortem” exercises in which
stakeholders identify the most likely events that could prevent a
project from achieving COD, financing milestones, or tax-credit
qualification. These exercises help teams proactively prioritize
mitigation strategies before risks become critical path issues.
Front-Loaded Diligence
In renewable energy transactions, unresolved mineral issues
discovered late in the financing process can jeopardize closing
timelines, increase curative costs, and create significant lender
concerns. Successful projects rely on front-loaded diligence and
proactive negotiation long before financing milestones are reached.
Experienced ALTA surveyors can play an important role during project
closings by coordinating directly with title teams, responding to
underwriting comments, revising certifications, and helping resolve
boundary or access issues that arise during final financing review.
Local and regional experience matters significantly in renewable
transactions. Surveyors and title professionals familiar with
county-level practices, local access issues, historical land use
patterns, and jurisdiction-specific requirements can often identify
risks and resolve issues more efficiently than firms lacking regional
expertise.
Government Agency Timing Risk and Transaction Delays
Compressed acquisition timelines create unique challenges when
renewable energy projects involve state or local government land. Unlike
private transactions, public-sector approvals often require multiple
layers of internal review, legal oversight, and administrative
coordination that do not always align with commercial financing
schedules.
Developers frequently underestimate how significantly government
processes can affect transaction timing. Even relatively straightforward
agreements involving access easements, road crossings, school trust
lands, water districts, or county-owned parcels may require review by
agency counsel, governing boards, procurement departments, or state
attorneys general before final approval can be granted. These review
processes are rarely accelerated to accommodate financing deadlines or
acquisition schedules.
Timing Risk is Often Administrative
Public agencies managing renewable energy requests are often
balancing competing priorities with limited personnel and aging
administrative systems. As a result, seemingly minor revisions to legal
descriptions, insurance requirements, or agreement formatting can create
unexpected delays late in the transaction process.
Projects involving checkerboard ownership patterns add another layer
of complexity. Different parcels within the same project footprint may
involve separate agencies, overlapping jurisdictions, or inconsistent
review standards. Developers may complete diligence on privately
controlled land only to discover that a single state-owned access
corridor or utility crossing remains unresolved. Because these parcels
often involve critical infrastructure or interconnection routes,
unresolved government approvals can quickly become financing
blockers.
To manage these risks effectively, developers should identify all
government-controlled parcels early in the diligence process and
prioritize approvals involving access roads, substations, collector
systems, and transmission corridors. Public-sector approvals should be
treated as critical path items rather than secondary administrative
tasks.
Successful transaction teams also recognize the importance of
relationship management during compressed timelines. Open communication
with agency staff, title professionals, surveyors, and legal reviewers
can help identify procedural issues early and prevent avoidable delays.
In many cases, understanding how an agency operates internally can be
just as important as understanding the legal requirements
themselves.
Administrative review, agency coordination, and public-sector
approval timelines can materially affect acquisition schedules,
financing certainty, and commercial operation deadlines. Projects that
anticipate these constraints early are far better positioned to maintain
momentum and achieve successful closings.
Real World Considerations
Exclusivity agreements are commonly signed during fast-paced
negotiations. The acquiring party must identify all issues within the
set timeframe. The first thing that we recommend is to understand the
intent of the transaction. What is the reason for acquiring the project?
Is it market share? Is the aim to invest in this technology? Is it for
cash flow? It is very important to understand the reason for the
acquisition, because that will guide many of your transactions.
We recommend prioritizing key parcels or areas to manage tight time
frames. Begin by identifying project improvements and locating your
medium voltage. Where is your high voltage? Where is your
interconnection? Where is your substation? Where is your access? Using
that as a guide to identify key parcels is extremely important. It is
also important to understand high risk issues as it relates to the
client. This varies from project to project. M&A deals can happen
early on. It’s just a matter of site control, but some clients want
later stage projects. The risk profile varies depending on the stage of
shovel-ready projects.
Managing Title Curative to Preserve Financing Timelines
Many developers utilize consolidated title review or “Red Light”
reports to centralize title exceptions, survey encroachments, lease
expirations, and unresolved curative items into a single tracking
framework. These reports help transaction teams prioritize critical
issues and coordinate cure strategies across legal, survey, title, and
development teams.
The A/B/C Curative Ranking Framework Critical (A) Financing blockers Lease failures Chain-of-title gaps Primary parcel defects Important (B) Lender holdback risks Moderate encroachments Subordination issues Low-Risk (C) Peripheral defects Escrow candidates Long-tail issues
Another important consideration is leveraging existing documents.
Know what’s in the data room. Someone should be auditing the data room
and making sure to note any gaps in the information. Ask for everything.
This is a critical time to make sure that information is shared.
We recommend assembling a multidisciplinary team, the composition of
the team will vary from project to project. Having the right experts,
both internally and externally is critical. Ensure that everyone
understands their responsibilities and that they communicate with one
another so that no details are overlooked. Ensure they understand all
relevant issues.
We are often tapped to be part of the team of experts who will be
examining the title, looking at mineral rights, and looking at site
control. When assembling your team, it is important that everyone
understands who is responsible for each part of the due diligence. They
need to know the critical deadlines and the focus of the work. Though it
may seem simple, team members often lack clarity on key risk factors and
when to share essential information during transactions. Make sure that
there is regular communication with stakeholders, to review due
diligence responsibilities and engage in problem solving.
Verifying Information is Critical
A clear example is a recent case where the seller was asked about a
permitting issue, he said: “Don’t worry, it’s all taken care of. Not a
problem.” Down the road, when project construction was about to begin,
they discovered that the permitting issue had not been resolved. This
caused unexpected delays and significant costs. Make sure to get all the
information and documentation you need from the prospective seller, then
conduct your own due diligence. Best practices will often standardize
processes, so that everything is consistent, and everyone is
informed.
Title review conducted under compressed transaction timelines carries
significant underwriting risk. Public records may be incomplete,
outdated, or inaccurate, and rushed diligence can result in overlooked
lines, easements, mineral severances, or ownership defects. These
omissions can create substantial downstream impact including title
claims, financing delays, increased curative costs, and litigation
exposure. Structured review procedures, experienced title professionals,
and standardized diligence processes help reduce the likelihood of
material issues being missed during fast-moving transactions.
Haste Makes Waste
Incomplete title searches create hidden transaction risks. Time pressure increases the likelihood of overlooked
encumbrances. Public records may be inaccurate or incomplete. Rushed diligence increases downstream litigation and claim
exposure. Experienced reviewers and standardized review procedures reduce
risk.
Mineral Ownership Reports (MORs) should be ordered early in the
diligence process, particularly in jurisdictions with active oil and gas
development or historical severances. Mineral ownership analysis often
requires extensive historical research and can materially impact
underwriting timelines, financing certainty, and project layout
decisions.
Strategies for Due Diligence Under Time Constraints - Prioritize Key
Areas
Critical Parcels: Focus on land essential for
project infrastructure. High-Risk Issues: Identify areas with potential
legal or environmental complications.
Examine Existing Documentation:
Review Sellers Data: Conduct a comprehensive review
of all documentation provided by the seller. Identify Gaps: Note missing or incomplete
information for follow-up.
Identify Stakeholders
Landowners, residents, community groups, and government agencies are
key stakeholders. Consider who is impacted by, interested in, or can
influence the project.
Focus your initial efforts on landowners whose property is central to
the project’s feasibility and potential construction footprint.
Engage with Landowners
To effectively engage landowners during renewable energy project due
diligence, identify all relevant stakeholders, establish transparent and
consistent communication through various channels and platforms. Inquire
about any unrecorded agreements, mineral rights, and environmental
concerns. Seek opportunities to build trust and to give landowners a
sense of ownership and involvement in the project. Maintain consistency
and follow-through.
Timing and Narrative Control
The earliest public narrative surrounding a project can significantly
influence community perception and permitting outcomes. Delayed
engagement or reactive communication strategies may allow opposition
groups to frame the project negatively before developers establish trust
with local stakeholders.
Establish Transparent Communication Channels
Employ a range of communication methods, including one-on-one
meetings, community forums, online platforms and informational
materials. Always be open and honest. Clearly communicate the project’s
purpose, potential benefits, environmental considerations, and any
potential impacts on land and community life.
We have seen so many projects where the developer has not controlled
the messaging. If you don’t control the messaging for your project,
others will and that could be a disaster. This is especially true with
social media. Has anything about the project been posted on social
media? Make sure you know what has been posted. Is the information
truthful? If not, you will need to have conversations with stakeholders
to discuss their concerns. Opposition to the project must be understood
and included in your due diligence reporting or risk potential
litigation.
Address Concerns Proactively
Provide clear information on how potential issues, such as noise,
visual impact, or land access, will be mitigated during construction and
operation.
Conduct Thorough Engagement Activities
Get feedback, use surveys, feedback forms, and open discussions to
understand landowners’ specific needs, concerns, and perspectives
regarding the project.
Document and Respond
Maintain comprehensive documentation of all communications and
feedback, ensuring that commitments made to landowners are fulfilled and
appropriately addressed.
Utilize Public Resources
Online Databases: Access property records,
environmental data, and GIS maps. Regulatory Agencies: Reach out to local authorities
for zoning and permitting information.
Assemble a Multidisciplinary Team Including an ALTA Surveyor
The Multidisciplinary Diligence Team Title Survey Legal Environmental Everyone knows their role, the deadline, and who else needs the information
The ALTA surveyor is a critical transaction partner in renewable
energy development and project finance. ALTA surveys are frequently
required for construction financing, tax equity transactions, title
insurance endorsements, and final project closings. Selecting an
experienced surveyor early in the diligence process can significantly
improve coordination between developers, title companies, lenders, and
underwriting teams while reducing closing delays. Use these criteria to
select the right surveyor:
Familiarity with state/county requirements Experience with renewable projects Ability to meet financing timelines Understanding Table A requirements Ability to support title endorsements Closing support experience Coordination with title underwriters
Internal collaboration should include the legal, development,
environmental, and engineering teams. External experts include
consultants for specialized assessments.
Project financing transactions require close coordination between
legal counsel, surveyors, title professionals, underwriting teams, and
financial stakeholders. Misalignment among these groups can create
delays, duplicate curative work, and unnecessary transaction risk.
Implement Technology Solutions
Data Management Tools: Use platforms that allow for
efficient document review and collaboration. Automated Alerts: Set up notifications for critical
deadlines and tasks.
Managing Title Curative Under Tight Transaction Timelines
Title curative Is the linchpin of financing. It is one of the most
important yet underestimated components of renewable energy M&A and
project finance. Unresolved title defects can delay financing, trigger
lender holdbacks, impact tax equity schedules, and jeopardize COD
targets. Effective curative management requires a structured process for
identifying, prioritizing, tracking, and resolving defects well before
closing.
The A / B / C Defect Ranking System
Critical (A)
Financing blockers Lease failures Primary parcel defects Title gaps
Important (B)
Lender holdback risks Subordination issues Moderate encroachments
Low Risk (C)
Long-tail risks Peripheral parcels Escrow candidates
Maximizing Efficiency
Standardized Processes: Develop checklists and
templates to streamline tasks. Regular Communication: Hold frequent team meetings
to track progress and address issues promptly. Delegate: Assign tasks based on expertise to ensure
efficiency.
An energy company successfully completed due diligence within a
60-day window by prioritizing critical leases and utilizing a
specialized team to focus on high-risk areas, thereby avoiding potential
delays in project development. While time constraints pose challenges,
strategic planning and efficient processes enable thorough due
diligence, reducing the risk of unforeseen complications
post-acquisition.

section: Environmental and Site Considerations in Project Acquisitions
text:
Environmental factors are critical in determining a project’s
feasibility, impacting not only the site’s suitability but also
regulatory compliance, community acceptance and long-term viability.
Environmental Site Assessment
Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) Flow Site Inspection & records review Biodiversity, Water, Soil & Air Analysis Risk Assessment Environmental Management Plan (EMP)
An Environmental Site Assessment (ESA) for a renewable energy project
is critical. The site assessment identifies potential environmental
impacts and includes site inspections, reviews of historical records,
government agency research, and analysis of factors such as
biodiversity, land use, water resources, soil conditions, and local
socio-economic impacts. The environmental site assessment also
establishes the presence of hazardous materials and evaluates risks to
human health and the environment, including water safety and air
quality. An expert assessment ensures that potential negative impacts
are identified, minimized or avoided before project development
proceeds.
Key Components of an Environmental Site Assessment
An environmental site assessment involves a visual inspection of the
site and a thorough review of property records to identify past land
uses and potential environmental concerns. This includes the
following:
Government Agency Records Research
Information is gathered from government agencies to identify
regulatory requirements, environmental constraints, and records of
environmental issues on or near the property.
Physical and Ecological Characteristics
The assessment evaluates the site’s suitability for the project,
considering existing land uses, soil conditions, and topography.
Biological Environment
Impacts on wildlife, plants, and overall biodiversity are
assessed.
Water Resources:
Water bodies, groundwater, and potential impacts on water quality are
evaluated.
Air Quality
The project’s potential effects on local air quality are considered.
For example, a California appeals court recently ruled that Kern County
violated CEQA (California Environmental Quality Act) with a flawed
environmental review for its oil and gas ordinance. Permitting was
halted until the ordinance was brought into compliance. This underscores
how local rules can override or delay development, even on privately
held mineral estates.
Human Health
Potential impacts on human health and public safety are analyzed.
Cultural Heritage
Any effects on cultural heritage sites are assessed.
Community Impact
The assessment considers potential effects on the local community,
including environmental justice issues.
Hazardous Materials and Contamination
The process identifies the presence of hazardous substances and
assesses whether on-site contaminants pose health or environmental
risks.
Risk Assessment
A comprehensive analysis of potential environmental risks is
conducted to inform mitigation strategies.
Environmental Management Plan (EMP)
The findings are used to develop a plan for managing and mitigating
environmental impacts during the project’s lifecycle, including
decommissioning.
Key Factors that Can Derail a Project
Many factors impact project development and viability. Next, we’ll
examine in greater detail key factors that can derail a project.
Flood Plains
Flooding can cause catastrophic damage to solar panels, inverters,
and other electrical equipment, potentially leading to system failure
and significant financial losses. Developing renewable energy projects
in floodplains requires flood risk assessment involving site selection,
flood-resilient design, and regulatory compliance to avoid damage,
ensure worker safety, and protect natural flood mitigation services.
Project development must consider elevated structures, flood-proof
electrical components, and the potential impact of infrastructure on the
natural flood control functions of floodplains, which are crucial for
ecosystems and water management.
Floods occur naturally and can happen almost anywhere. They may not
even be near a body of water, although river and coastal flooding are
two of the most common types. Heavy rains, poor drainage, and nearby
construction projects can put your project at risk for flood damage.
Always look at FEMA maps. FEMA maintains and updates data through flood
maps and risk assessments. Flood maps are one tool to know which areas
have the highest risk of flooding. Once you understand the potential
risk of flooding, you may need flood insurance.
Protected Species and Habitats
In addition to flood plains, there are other risks to examine.
Determine early if protected species or habitats are present on site.
Ask for biological assessments. Have wildlife agencies been contacted?
Have they presented any data or recommendations to ensure legal
compliance? If this information does not exist, contact relevant
agencies to conduct a site review.
Unexpected issues can arise if environmental studies are not
reviewed. For example, a wind energy project we worked on was delayed
when it was discovered that the site was a migratory pathway for
endangered birds. This meant that the developer had to implement
significant mitigation measures, including curtailment strategies and
habitat conservation plans, increasing costs and affecting
timelines.
Wetlands and Water Bodies
Wetlands provide a multitude of ecological, economic, and social
benefits. They supply habitats for diverse species, replenish
groundwater, limit flooding, purify drinking water, yield food and
fiber, and enable cultural and recreational activities. Projects
affecting wetlands may need Clean Water Act permits.
Identify wetlands using National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) maps. The
National Wetlands Inventory (NWI) was established by the U.S. Fish and
Wildlife Service (Service) to conduct a nationwide inventory of U.S.
wetlands to provide biologists, land management planners and others with
information on the distribution and type of wetlands.
Soil and Geotechnical Conditions
Soil and geotechnical condition reports are essential for renewable
energy projects, providing data on subsurface properties, soil strength,
and potential hazards to ensure safe and stable foundation design for
structures like wind turbines and solar arrays. These reports use field
investigations (e.g., boreholes, CPT) and laboratory tests to determine
soil characteristics, inform foundation selection, minimize risks, and
guarantee the long-term stability and performance of the energy
infrastructure.
Soil and geotechnical reports identify potential geotechnical hazards
(e.g., slope stability, soil strength, ground instability) that could
compromise the safety and longevity of the infrastructure. A thorough
report helps understand the site-specific geological and subsurface
conditions, including soil types, stratigraphy, and the presence of any
anomalies. Evaluating ground stability for transmission lines and
associated structures identifies potential ground settlement or other
issues.
Cultural and Historical Sites
Cultural and historical sites are crucial considerations in renewable
energy development because projects can impact historical sites,
indigenous lands, and culturally significant landscapes. Can disturb or
destroy archaeological sites containing artifacts, human remains, or
historic structures. Many significant cultural and sacred sites are
located on public or private land designated for renewable energy
projects, leading to potential conflicts over land use and access. This
can require archaeological surveys, community consultation, and impact
assessments to avoid destruction and ensure respectful development
practices.
Development on tribal lands requires compliance with federal, tribal,
and state laws, and usually needs tribal or landowner approval. Federal
agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) issue
environmental permits for sources on tribal lands, and the Bureau of
Indian Affairs (BIA) handles leases and right-of-way grants. Tribes can
often develop their own permitting programs and may need to meet
specific criteria to qualify.
We once worked on a project in Wyoming where we conducted our own
site review. We saw what looked to us like piles of rocks. Engaging
local stakeholders revealed these were protected historical and cultural
tribal artifacts. We had to negotiate with various groups, including
tribal leaders and local landowners, to create easements that permit the
tribes access to the sacred site to conduct their vision quests.
Easements for all stakeholders to both the property and the project had
to be designed. Understanding those rights and making sure that you deal
with them early on is extremely important.
The visual character of a landscape can also be culturally
significant. Large-scale wind turbines or extensive solar arrays can
dramatically alter the aesthetic and historic qualities of a region,
often leading to community opposition.
Health Protection Zones
We had a project in California where there are Health Protection
Zones. Health Protection Zones are instituted by the county. These are
large areas that do not allow any improvements. In California, “Health
Protection Zones” (HPZs) are specific 3,200-foot buffer zones
established around sensitive receptors (e.g., homes, schools, hospitals)
intended to protect communities from industrial hazards. The 3,200 feet
is measured from the property line of the sensitive receptor or the
building footprint, depending on the setback distance. Rather than
dictating general building practices, these zones strictly regulate the
proximity and operations of the oil and gas industry.
Jurisdictions like Illinois have health protection zones within
vicinity of the city. These factors are crucial, if you’re purchasing a
200 MW project or a 1000 MW portfolio, you don’t want to discover
significant land use issues after land acquisition. That is another
reason that environmental site assessments and community engagement are
an important part of due diligence. Get to know the leaders and the
influencers of the community, they can provide you with insights that
can help you to more effectively identify potential issues.
Community Acceptance
Community acceptance has really moved up the ladder in terms of
importance in transactions. Resistance to renewable energy projects
stems from a wide range of concerns, including environmental impact,
economic fears, and aesthetic objections. This is compounded by issues
like a lack of early engagement, insufficient information, and distrust
in developers or project governance. Overcoming this resistance requires
early community dialogue, clear communication of project benefits and
potential local gains, addressing specific concerns, and establishing
long-term trust through local empowerment and commitment from developers
and governing bodies.
Community engagement should be treated as a core component of project
risk management rather than a secondary public relations function. Early
engagement, consistent communication, and proactive stakeholder outreach
can materially reduce permitting delays, litigation risk, and
transaction uncertainty. Conduct online research and speak with
community leaders to gain clarity and build support.
Navigating Tribal Lands and Sovereign Jurisdictions
Renewable energy development on tribal lands involves unique legal,
regulatory, and governance considerations because federally recognized
tribes operate as sovereign nations. Tribal lands are frequently held in
trust by the federal government, and project development may require
approvals, procedures, and enforceability considerations that differ
substantially from conventional private-land transactions.
Tribal governance structures, leadership transitions, and community
priorities may evolve during project development, making trust,
transparency, and consistent engagement critical components of
successful project execution.
Bureau of Indian Affairs (BIA) Approval Risk
Tribal Land & BIA Approval Timeline Risk Lease / Easement Executed by parties BIA Review Additional approval layer Legally Effective Only after BIA approval Build this extra approval step into financing & construction schedules
Many tribal land agreements require post-execution approval from the
Bureau of Indian Affairs. As a result, executed leases, assignments,
easements, or surface agreements may not become legally effective until
federal approval is obtained. Developers and acquirers should
incorporate these additional approval timelines into project schedules,
financing assumptions, and transaction risk assessments.
Opposition Risk Is a Material Development Risk
Community opposition has evolved into a significant project
development and transaction risk within the renewable energy sector. In
many jurisdictions, organized opposition groups have successfully
delayed or blocked utility-scale renewable projects with political
campaigns, public hearings, litigation threats, and social media
activism. These risks can materially affect permitting certainty,
development timelines, financing schedules, and project valuation.
Developers should be prepared to address misinformation, community
concerns, and rapidly evolving public narratives surrounding renewable
energy projects. Social media and organized opposition campaigns can
accelerate public resistance if stakeholder engagement is delayed or
inconsistent.
Stakeholder Segmentation
Developers should recognize that local communities are rarely
homogeneous. Stakeholders often include landowners benefiting from lease
revenue, local businesses expecting economic activity, government
entities anticipating tax revenue, and residents who perceive little or
no direct benefit from the project. Effective engagement strategies
should be tailored to each group’s interests, concerns, and
motivations.
Case Study – Migratory Birds A wind energy project was delayed when it was discovered that the
site was a migratory pathway for endangered birds. The developer had to
implement mitigation measures, including curtailment strategies and
habitat conservation plans, increasing costs and affecting timelines.
Environmental due diligence and community engagement are not just about
compliance but also about ensuring the long-term viability and
acceptance of the project.
Community engagement recommendations contributed by Ayelet Hines
& Mike Casey, Tigercomm.

title: Chapter 7: Hidden Layers - Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project Acquisitions
section:
Hidden Layers - Addressing Complex Ownership Structures in Project
Acquisitions
text:
M&A has become one of the fastest ways to fill pipeline gaps in
the renewable sector. With interconnection queues stretching for years
and greenfield development slowing under regulatory and community
pressure, acquiring projects can be the most effective path forward. But
there’s a catch. Deals that look strong on paper can fall apart during
closing. The reason? Risks are often buried in the details, such as land
ownership issues or missing signatures that weren’t uncovered early
enough.
Every deal carries risk. The question is whether you identify those
risks early, when they can be managed, or later, when they threaten
valuation and delay closing of the deal.
Ownership structures can be intricate, with various interests that
may not be immediately apparent. Companies often form partnerships to
develop projects. This requires a clear understanding of the agreements,
Identifying and resolving these complexities is essential to securing
valid agreements.
Hidden Ownership Complexities
Ownership isn’t always straightforward. Overlooking a single
signatory can render a lease unenforceable. Unrecorded rights, which
often exist, can completely derail financing. Common ownership issues
include:
Life Estates: If the life tenant hasn’t signed, the
agreements are incomplete. Trusts & Estates: Require specific
authorization to bind the entity. Easements and rights-of-way allow third parties to
use parts of the property, potentially limiting development or requiring
adjustments. Undivided Interests: All co-owners must consent to
lease terms. Encumbrances and Liens: Claims by creditors or
other parties against the property, that need to be resolved or
subordinated. Probate Complications: Missing heirs can stall
transactions for years. Off-record Agreements: Grazing leases, water
rights, or off-record access can create conflicts.
It is critical to look beyond the deed. Confirm signatory authority,
identify any unrecorded interests through landowner conversations. Don’t
assume that what is disclosed in the title report tells the whole story.
Let’s examine frequently encountered complexities in greater detail.
Life Estates
Life Estate: Two Interests, One Property Life Tenant Possesses & uses property for their lifetime Remainderman Receives full ownership upon tenant's death at death
A life estate is a legal ownership interest in real property that
lasts for the duration of a person’s life, known as the “life tenant.”
This arrangement divides ownership into two interests: the right to
possess and use the property during the tenant’s lifetime and the right
to receive the property after their death, called the “remainderman.”
The life tenant cannot leave the property to their heirs, as their
interest automatically ends upon their death.
The remainderman is the individual or party who receives full
ownership of the property after the life tenant’s death. For example, a
deed might read, “To John Doe for life, then to Jane Doe.” In this case,
John receives a life estate and can use the property during his
lifetime. Upon John’s death, Jane Doe automatically receives full
ownership of the property.
The duration of the life estate is measured by the life of the life
tenant, or another specified person (known as a life estate pur autre
vie). The individual holding lifetime rights, which is the life tenant,
must provide his or her consent to leases or agreements affecting their
interest. Therefore, it is imperative that the life tenant’s signature
is on all agreements related to their property.
Trusts & Estates
Trust Structure: Three Stakeholders Grantor Trust managed by Trustee Beneficiary Trustee must verify authority & terms before signing any agreement
A trust is a legal arrangement established to manage and distribute
assets. Ownership of those assets moves from the original owner to the
trust. The person or organization managing the trust takes on a
fiduciary role, protecting the assets to the benefit of the
beneficiaries. The trust sets conditions that must be met for the assets
to eventually transfer from the trust to its beneficiaries.
There are three types of stakeholders involved in a trust:
The grantor. This is the person who places their
assets into the trust. The trustee. The trustee oversees the assets in the
trust. They enter into the agreement knowing that they must manage those
assets in the best interests of the beneficiaries. The beneficiary or beneficiaries. Assuming the
conditions of the trust are met, the beneficiaries receive the assets
held in that trust.
There are several types of trusts, categories include revocable
trusts (can be changed by the grantor while alive) and irrevocable
trusts (difficult or impossible to change once established).
Establishing a trust allows the grantor and their beneficiaries to avoid
probate court. Probate can cause major delays, because all heirs must
sign documents related to transactions. Assets are held in a trust are
no longer part of an individual’s estate. Trust property requires
trustee action and verification of both their authority and the terms of
trust.
Estate generally refers to the total assets and liabilities (debts) a
person or legal entity owns at a particular point in time, or upon
death. However, the specific legal definition can vary depending on the
context and scope of the estate.
Easements and Rights-of-Way
An easement is a legal right for a non-owner to use another person’s
land for a specific purpose, while a right-of-way is a specific type of
easement that grants the right to travel or pass across another person’s
property. All rights-of-way are easements, but not all easements are
rights-of-way, as easements can also cover purposes like the flow of
utilities or support for structures. A right to use someone else’s land
for a specific purpose without owning it. The scope of an easement can
be broad, encompassing various uses such as installing utility lines,
allowing support for a shared wall, or providing access to water.
A right-of-way is a legal easement that allows individuals to travel
across or over another person’s property. It facilitates movement across
land for a specific beneficiary or purpose. Easements can be for
utilities, support, or access, whereas rights-of-way are exclusively for
travel or passage. Easement is a broader category, while a right-of-way
is a narrower, specific type of easement focused on access and
passage.
In Illinois for example, renewable energy projects rely on private
land easements and public right-of-way (ROW) agreements. Landowners
typically negotiate voluntary lease and easement agreements with
developers, often guided by the state’s Illinois Department of
Agriculture and state setback rules to safeguard agricultural land and
local drainage. Navigating these agreements in Illinois requires an
understanding of several critical factors:
Agricultural Impact Mitigation Agreements
(AIMAs)
Developers of large-scale wind and solar farms are required to
negotiate an AIMA with the Illinois Department of Agriculture before
construction. This ensures that productive farmland is restored to its
pre-construction capabilities, protecting soil compaction, and securing
just compensation for crop losses.
Easement Types
Projects require multiple easements. These include access easements
for roads, utility easements for underground and overhead transmission
lines, and “solar/wind rights” easements that prohibit adjacent property
owners from building tall structures or planting trees that could block
sunlight or wind.
Right-of-Way (ROW)
Developers frequently need to cross, occupy, or tie into public road
rights-of-way. Under the state’s model ordinances, wind turbines are
typically required to be set back at least 1.1 times their maximum blade
tip height from the center point of public road rights-of-way.
State Setback & Drainage Protections
Recent legislation limits local control to reasonable regulations,
meaning municipalities cannot outright ban renewable development.
Facility owners are also authorized to cross drainage systems and
drainage tiles during construction, provided they restore the land as
soon as practicable.
Illinois offers just one example of the complexities of easements and
rights-of-way. Always check with each state and county for comprehensive
guidelines on hosting renewable infrastructure.
Undivided Interests
An undivided interest is a form of shared ownership where multiple
parties hold rights to an entire property, rather than a specific
portion of it. Each co-owner has an equal right to possess and enjoy the
whole property, but their ownership is defined by a percentage share of
the total asset. For instance, when three siblings inherit a property,
each person possesses a one-third undivided interest in the entire
residence. This means that all co-owners must agree to the terms of the
lease or sale of the property.
Encumbrances and Liens
An encumbrance refers to a claim on a property that limits the
owner’s ability to use it. A lien is a particular category of
encumbrance, representing a financial claim intended to secure repayment
of a debt. Encumbrances can also be non-financial, such as an easement
that allows someone else to use a portion of the property, or a deed
restriction that limits how the property can be developed. Claims by
creditors or other parties against the property may need to be resolved
or subordinated.
Probate Complications
Missing or unlocatable heirs are a significant complication in
probate. The executor must locate and inform all beneficiaries before
any assets can be distributed. This can lead to substantial delays,
potentially stalling transactions for years and requiring extensive
efforts like skip tracing. In probate, skip tracing means finding
hard-to-locate beneficiaries, witnesses, or other parties to ensure they
are properly notified or can provide needed information for
administering the estate. This can be a complex and time-consuming
process, especially for large or complex estates where family trees are
extensive and members may be estranged or living in different
jurisdictions. Probate complications impact mineral rights searches as
well.
The court has a legal obligation to ensure all beneficiaries are
notified of the probate proceedings. This requirement creates a
mandatory pause in the process until all heirs are found or a reasonable
effort to locate them has been exhausted.
Off-record Agreements
Unrecorded agreements related to property use such as grazing leases,
water rights, or off-record access can create conflicts. These
agreements may be legally binding between the parties involved, yet they
lack public notice and can create issues for buyers or lenders who are
unaware of the rights or restrictions, potentially leading to
conflicting ownership claims or title defects.
Strategies for Unveiling and Addressing Complexities
Title Examination
Review the chain of title and all recorded documents. Identify all
parties with a legal interest in the property. Engage real estate
attorneys experienced in complex ownership issues who can interpret
legal documents and advise on necessary actions.
Owner Communication
Directly contact owners to understand unrecorded interests or
agreements. Use questionnaires to gather detailed information.
Verification of Authority
Obtain documentation proving individuals have the authority to sign,
such as power of attorney, trustee certification or the like.
Negotiation and Resolution
Proactively address any disputes or claims. Negotiate terms that are
acceptable to all parties.
Risks of Overlooking Ownership Complexities
Invalid Agreements: Missing consents can render leases
unenforceable.
Project Delays: Time required to resolve issues can impact
timelines.
Financial Implications: Additional costs for legal fees, settlements,
or project redesign.
Real-World Example A solar project was halted when a previously unknown easement allowed
a utility company to install transmission lines across the property,
conflicting with the project’s layout. The developer had to renegotiate
with the utility, causing delays and additional costs.
Thoroughly investigating and addressing ownership complexities
ensures that the project’s legal foundation is sound and reduces the
risk of future disputes.
